name: West Futuna
confidence_why: Dougherty 1983, the reference grammar by the principal fieldworker (restating her 1977 rule), assigns stress to the penultimate vowel with a word-final vowel sequence counting as one syllable, and Capell 1984's independently compiled dictionary grammar concurs that penultimate stress is the usual pattern with antepenultimate on consonant-plus-ia verbs and final stress on vowel-cluster-final words, differing only over one word ('star') and some free variation, so two independent descriptions agree.

catalog_quote: Stress can be assigned for the majority of West Futuna words by a rule that places primary stress of the final syllable if it is a vowel dipthong and otherwise on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable depending upon the stem shape. The general rule for stress assignment is: V → V́ / __ [-syl]₀ V·(V) (Dougherty 1978) The raised dot indicates a syllable boundary. The subscript indicates that the number of nonsyllablic units which follow the stressed vowel is not specified. None, one or two such phones are attested in West Futuna speech. Examples include: /ké/ different, strange /úa/ rain /pái/ far /fíe/ firewood /úri/ dark /mága/ to branch /úta/ a load, cargo /utáina/ to load something /síko/ ... /sikófia/ ... /fesáo(a)/ to speak, to tell something /ámo(a)/ to take or carry something /hkánu/ stripe /arátu/ tomorrow /méntua/ to think or remember /móega/ clothing /amósia/ t…

new_statements.quote: [T]he statistically commonest type is the penultimate. There are more exceptions to the pattern in Aniwa than in Futuna because Aniwa often rejects final syllables that are present in Futuna, e.g. A. /am'ke/, F. /am'kea/ 'remove'; in some cases there seems to be a free variation ... both /fa'nua/ and /'fanua/ 'land' will be met with. Final stress is more usual in Aniwa than in Futuna. Antepenultimate stress is found in some words in both languages. Many of the examples are provided by the transitive form of the verb ending in -ia preceded by a consonant. In these the stress does not necessarily move forward with the addition of a syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's deciding source (Dougherty 1983 rule V → V́ / __ [-syl]0 V·(V), catalog classification weight-hedged): default penult, antepenult on consonant+ia/ua-final words, stress on the first vowel of a word-final vowel cluster. Capell adds what the catalog lacks: the Futuna-vs-Aniwa difference (more final stress and more exceptions in Aniwa), attested free variation, the pronoun antepenults, the near-absence of phonemic vowel length, and the sentence-level emphatic stress. Nothing contradicts the catalog at the system level; one lexical item differs (Capell F. /'fatu/ 'star' with initial stress vs Dougherty's lexically marked final-stress /fatú/ 'star').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress is the statistically commonest pattern in both Futuna and Aniwa (established from the texts, not a formal rule). Antepenultimate stress occurs in some words, chiefly transitive verbs in consonant + -ia where the stress stays put when the suffix syllable is added, and in some Futuna pronouns (/a'kitea/ 'we'). Final stress is more usual in Aniwa than in Futuna (Aniwa drops final syllables that Futuna keeps). Some free variation exists (/fa'nua/ ~ /'fanua/ 'land'; /'tukua/ ~ /tu'kua/ 'say', 1.1.2). Word-final diphthongs count as two-vowel clusters for stress: /ta'mau/ 'your father' is 'functionally /ta'ma-u/, with ultimate stress' (1.1.3.1.1), i.e. stress on the first vowel of the final cluster; non-final diphthongs function as single vowels. Vowel length is 'rarely phonemic' (/'fatu/ 'star' vs /'fa:tu/ 'stone', 1.1.3.0); consonant length is absent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress is stated. 1.1.3.1.2 treats sentence stress: emphatic word orders give a strong stress plus slight glottal closure on the emphasised word (e.g. /'?eia/ 'him'), and weak stress marks close juncture (a postposed actor /koua/ is 'so lightly stressed as almost to become part of the preceding action word').
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress in consonant+-ia transitives and in pronouns (/a'kitea/ 'we'; A. /a'kere/ ~ /a'kerea/ 'they'; Paton's 19th-century spelling 'acre' implies earlier /'akare/); final stress in Aniwa after final-syllable loss (A. /am'ke/ vs F. /am'kea/); free variation /fa'nua/ ~ /'fanua/, /'tukua/ ~ /tu'kua/; final diphthongs stressed on their first vowel (/ta'ma-u/).
new_statements.identity_note: Capell 1984 covers both dialects of Futuna-Aniwa and marks examples F. (Futuna) and A. (Aniwa); his stress statements about 'both languages' apply to West Futuna, and he says the final-stress pattern is more usual in Aniwa (Glottolog treats Aniwa as a dialect within futu1245). Dougherty 1977 is explicitly the West Futuna island variety (about 800 speakers, southern New Hebrides).

new_statements.quote: Stress is assigned by the following rule: [left-hand side illegible in the digitisation] → V — [-syl]0 V.(V)# where the raised dot (·) indicates a syllable boundary. /ké/ 'different, strange' /ôa/ 'rain' /pái/ 'far' /fíe/ 'firewood' /mága/ 'to branch' /utáina/ 'to load something' ... /arátu/ 'tomorrow' /amósia/ 'to rub or wipe something' /tamótua/ 'power, skill' /tavenága/ 'to discuss'. Exceptions to this generalisation are analysed synchronically as lexically marked for stress. At least one class of such exceptions derives historically from stems with a long vowel sequence with or without an intervening glottal stop. /afá/ 'storm, hurricane' < PPN /*afaa/ /fatô/ 'star' < PPN /*fetu'u/

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very rule the catalog's deciding source cites as 'Dougherty 1978' (Dougherty 1983 pp. 12-14): the same formula V → V́ / __ [-syl]0 V·(V)#, the same example list (ké.. tavenága) and the same 'lexically marked' exceptions with the PPN long-vowel etymologies. Identical placement; the article adds the reduplication facts (one major stress per reduplicated constituent; each repeated segment stressed) and the ordering of glide formation before stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A single rule: the stressed vowel is the one followed by zero or more non-syllabics and then the final vowel, which may itself be followed by one more vowel across a syllable boundary (V.(V)#). In effect stress is penultimate counting a word-final vowel sequence such as -ua/-ia/-oa as the last syllable: /mága/, /arátu/, /pái/, /fíe/ but /amósia/, /tamótua/, /méntua/, /fesáo(a)/ (surface antepenult before C+V.V#). Exceptions are lexically marked; one class carries final stress from historical long vowels (/afá/ < *afaa, /fatô/ [=/fatú/] 'star' < *fetu'u, /htô/ 'upright' < *tu'u), and a further listed set has unpredicted antepenult (/wárusia/, /lôkujia/, /mágaro/, /pákasi/, /átata/, /finágaro/). Glide formation (fn. 5) applies before stress assignment.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such. p. 209: a productively reduplicated form receives 'a single major stress assignment', whereas in repetition 'primary stress is assigned to each complete segment of a repeated series'; the derivation /fofóí+a/ (p. 212) shows two accent marks but the text does not call one of them secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked stress: final-stress class from PPN long vowels (/afá/, /fatô/, /htô/; fn. 2 /vahvá/, /tuhtô/ from /hvá/, /htô/); antepenult items /wárusia/, /lôkujia/, /mágaro/, /pákasi/, /átata/, /finágaro/; /píri+ji+a/ 'lexically marked stress' in the derivations p. 212. Recent loans keeping final consonants (/keresín/, /lét/, /krín/, /práon/) are stressed on their final closed syllable (fn. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Capell 1984 covers both dialects of Futuna-Aniwa and marks examples F. (Futuna) and A. (Aniwa); his stress statements about 'both languages' apply to West Futuna, and he says the final-stress pattern is more usual in Aniwa (Glottolog treats Aniwa as a dialect within futu1245). Dougherty 1977 is explicitly the West Futuna island variety (about 800 speakers, southern New Hebrides).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on the system: both works, and the catalog's deciding source (Dougherty 1983), put default stress on the penultimate vowel with a word-final vowel sequence counting as the final syllable (surface antepenult on C+ia/ua-final words such as /amósia/, /tamótua/), and both recognise a lexically marked residue of final stress from historical long vowels. Two small points of difference: (a) Capell gives F. /'fatu/ 'star' with initial stress (contrasting with /'fa:tu/ 'stone') where Dougherty lists /fatô/ (= /fatú/) 'star' < *fetu'u as lexically marked final stress; (b) Capell reports free variation (/fa'nua/ ~ /'fanua/ 'land', /'tukua/ ~ /tu'kua/ 'say') and more final stress in Aniwa, which Dougherty's single rule plus lexical marking does not model; Dougherty describes only the Futuna island variety. Neither point changes the placement type.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage, rule, example list and exceptions are verbatim on the page scan we hold of Dougherty 1983 pp.12-14 at exactly the stated locator. (2) Deciding source: a 1983 reference grammar by the principal fieldworker, Glottolog's only full grammar for futu1245; nothing later or more specialised appears in Glottolog's descriptive list, and the two other primary stress statements that exist (Dougherty 1977 JPS, the source of the rule; Capell 1984 PL C-56 section 1.1.3.1) were downloaded now from open copies and read. Both agree with the record: default penult, antepenult on consonant+ia/ua-final (transitive -ia) words, stress on the first vowel of a word-final falling diphthong, and a lexically marked final-stress class from historical long vowels. Capell refines rather than contradicts: he analyses final diphthongs as two-vowel clusters with stress on the penultimat
